extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political science; statesmen, journalists, and general readers interested in the nature of public opinion and democratic government
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and frames principles about how public opinion is formed, how it interacts with political leaders and institutions, and the strengths, dangers, and safeguards of government by public opinion. The material is a descriptive-normative treatment useful for assessing democratic systems and political practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass contribution is primarily sentiment rather than thought
rubrics_metrics.description: For the great mass of mankind public questions obtain less than a third or a fourth of the leisure available for thinking; it is therefore rather sentiment than thought that the mass can contribute, 'a sentiment grounded on a few broad considerations and simple trains of reasoning.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to evaluate popular reactions: expect broad, sentiment-driven judgments rather than detailed factual analysis. The soundness of mass sentiment depends more on appeals to justice, honour, and peace than on intricate reasoning; communications aimed at the mass should address broad considerations and simple trains of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educated/wealthy classes are influenced differently (interest and timidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The so-called upper or wealthier classes are less influenced by sentiment and more influenced by notions, often erroneous, of their own interest; possession of property makes a man timid and apt to underrate the power and worth of sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing elite opinion, account for property-based self-interest and cautiousness; do not assume superior analytical judgment simply from education or degrees. Messaging or policy that threatens perceived property or status may be resisted regardless of factual merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between passive and active opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Passive opinion: the opinion of those who receive or propagate but do not originate views on public matters (the nineteen out of twenty). Active opinion: the class of persons who occupy themselves primarily with public affairs and aspire to create and lead opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses of public opinion should separate spontaneous mass sentiment (passive) from manufactured or led opinion (active). Tactics differ: passive opinion spreads 'spontaneously and naturally,' while active opinion is consciously made and subject to leaders' incentives and constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders (statesmen, journalists) must 'sound the general opinion' before committing
rubrics_metrics.description: A statesman or journalist is usually on the alert to sound the general opinion before he commits himself on a new issue; he tries to feel the pulse of the mass of average citizens because if he stands aloof he may lose influence and position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical political action often requires leaders to test and adapt to popular feeling. Evaluate leaders' decisions by whether they appropriately gauge popular receptivity and balance individual judgment with the risk of isolation or losing effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual action and reaction of leaders and the mass shapes opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The mutual action and reaction of the makers or leaders of opinion upon the mass, and of the mass upon them, is the most curious part of the process by which opinion is produced; proportions of influence vary by country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing opinion formation, consider the two-way dynamics: leaders initiate ideas that the mass modifies, accentuates, or rejects, producing a final public opinion different from either pure leadership or pure mass sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion underlies governmental legitimacy and stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments have always rested, and must rest, if not on affection then on reverence or awe, if not on active approval then on silent acquiescence of the numerical majority; even despotisms often depend on popular assent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the legitimacy and durability of regimes by the degree of popular assent (active or passive). The absence of explicit resistance often masks reliance on habit, custom, or religious sanction; legitimacy is not solely coercive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages in the evolution of public opinion (passive → active → representative → continuous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three stages: (1) opinion acquiesces in will of ruler (passive); (2) conflicts and revolutions arise as people awaken; (3) the former ruler submits and disputes are referred to the sovereign multitude via representatives. A possible fourth stage is continuous ascertainability of the majority's will without representative intermediaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this framework to classify a polity's level of public-consciousness and institutional development. The stage indicates appropriate institutions and potential frictions (e.g., conflicts during transition from stage 2 to 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical difficulties of a government governed directly by continuous public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: How is the will of the majority to be ascertained except by counting votes? How, without the greatest inconvenience, can votes be frequently taken on all chief questions? No large country has yet surmounted these inconveniences (Switzerland and some American states being partial exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing direct mechanisms to capture popular will, evaluate logistical feasibility, frequency, and cost—referendums and initiatives address some issues but also have limits. Practical governance must reckon with measurement and timing constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk: difficulty of honestly ascertaining the majority's will (fraud, bribery, force)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the issues are weighty the danger of bribery, of force, and still more of fraud in taking and counting votes is serious; when ballots have been tampered with the value of the system is gone and men revert to older methods of settling differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess democratic mechanisms for robustness against fraud and coercion; legitimacy depends on honest, reliable electoral procedures. Systems must be scrutinized for vulnerabilities when high stakes are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk: suppression or demoralization of minorities under strong majority sway
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a majority has erred, the only remedy is continued protests and agitation of the minority; but the more complete the sway of majorities, the less disposed a minority is to maintain contest—losing faith and allowing its voice to be silenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a democracy's health by the ease with which minorities can sustain dissent: look for safe, energetic channels for protest (voice and pen) and institutional protections that keep majorities from ossifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative role of the patriotic statesman: resist and correct dominant sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of a patriotic statesman in a country where public opinion rules would seem to be rather to resist and correct than to encourage the dominant sentiment; he will confront it, lecture it, remind it that it is fallible, rouse it out of self-complacency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging leaders, consider their willingness to challenge popular but mistaken sentiment. Courage and independence are virtues that must be cultivated to check majoritarian excesses; their absence is a democratic risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural safeguards: limit popular powers by time and method; parcel functions among many agents
rubrics_metrics.description: One plan is for the people themselves to limit their powers by surrounding action with restrictions of time and method which compel delay. Another is to parcel out functions among many agents so that no single chosen indiscreetly can do much mischief and differences of view may arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional design should include time-lags, procedural checks, and fragmented authority to mitigate rash majoritarian action. Use constitutional limits, staggered terms, and distributed decision-making to reduce risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural safeguards: temper and character of the people (individuality, moral sense, diversity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A country that has worked out truly free government must have done so by virtue of vigorous individuality; a keen moral sense and capacity for strong emotions mean opinion based on love of what is just or good will resist a majority bent on evil. Variety of social conditions and religious beliefs serve as centres of resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the informal cultural conditions supporting democracy: civic vitality, moral intensity in minorities, and social pluralism are important protective factors beyond formal institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency over time: longer rule of public opinion increases majority authority and reduces energetic minorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The longer public opinion has ruled the more absolute is the authority of the majority likely to become, the less likely are energetic minorities to arise, and the more politicians are likely to occupy themselves in discovering and obeying opinion rather than forming it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider historical trajectory when assessing democratic resilience: entrenched majoritarian habits can produce complacency and a decline in dissenting vigor; monitor incentives for political actors to lead versus follow public sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of popular government (classification and implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three forms: (1) primary assemblies where the whole people meets (ancient Greek, Swiss cantons); (2) representative bodies (Parliaments) with relatively long tenures (English model); (3) hybrid between the two where legislatures are elected for short times and ultimate authority resides with the people (United States).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to diagnose institutional choices and their implications for directness of control, frequency of accountability, and the balance between deliberation and responsiveness. Each form has trade-offs in scale, practicality, and susceptibility to majority error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of the American system as an example of government by public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States exemplifies the third form: Congress sits for two years, is strictly limited by the Constitution, the Federal executive is directly named by and responsible to the people; legislatures sit for short periods and people frequently legislate directly by enacting or altering constitutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating American-style systems, focus on short representative terms, constitutional limits, state-federal balance, and direct popular mechanisms. These features intensify direct popular sovereignty but also raise specific vulnerabilities (e.g., constitutional rigidity at the federal level).
